name: Hammurabi
summary: Sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon (r. c. 1792–1750 BCE), he turned a small city-state into an empire covering most of Mesopotamia through diplomacy and war against Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari. His letters show a king closely involved in canals, taxes and court cases.

He is credited with the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft, economics, law, espionage and war, rediscovered in 1905. His realism has led to comparisons with Machiavelli. Legends also attribute aphorisms (Chanakya Niti) to him.

name: Panini
summary: Panini, a grammarian from Shalatula near Gandhara (around the 5th–4th century BCE), wrote the Ashtadhyayi, about 4,000 concise rules (sutras) describing Sanskrit's sounds, word formation and syntax. His system uses meta-rules, recursion and abbreviations similar to modern formal languages; the Backus–Naur form used in computer science is sometimes called Panini–Backus form. His grammar standardised Classical Sanskrit.

name: Archimedes
summary: Archimedes (about 287–212 BCE) of Syracuse in Sicily was the greatest mathematician of antiquity. He approximated π, calculated areas and volumes using methods close to integral calculus, discovered the principle of buoyancy (reportedly shouting 'Eureka!' in his bath), and explained levers ('Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth'). He designed war machines to defend Syracuse against Rome and was killed by a Roman soldier during the city's fall.

summary: Sushruta, a physician traditionally said to have taught at Kashi (Varanasi) around the 6th century BCE (the text took shape over centuries), is credited with the Sushruta Samhita. It describes over 300 surgical procedures and 120 instruments, including rhinoplasty using a cheek or forehead flap, cataract surgery and treatment of fractures, and recommends practising on gourds and dead animals. He is called the 'father of surgery'.

name: Aryabhata
summary: Aryabhata (476–550 CE) wrote the Aryabhatiya at age 23 in Kusumapura (Pataliputra) during the Gupta era. He used place-value notation, approximated π as 3.1416, gave sine tables, and proposed that the Earth rotates on its axis, explaining the apparent motion of the stars. He explained solar and lunar eclipses through shadows rather than the demon Rahu. India's first satellite (1975) was named after him.

name: Brahmagupta
summary: Brahmagupta (598–668), from Bhinmal in Rajasthan, wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628), the first text to treat zero as a number with rules for arithmetic: a number minus itself is zero; negative times negative is positive.
